lenses.name: Economics
lenses.question: Who pays, who benefits, and what does the marginal unit cost?
lenses.body: Under this lens a problem is a ledger. Nodes about cost, incentive, and who captures the benefit come into focus.

lenses.name: Statistics & ML
lenses.question: What data exists, what is the scoring function, and how would it be gamed?
lenses.body: Under this lens every node becomes a question about data, a score, and a holdout. Platt's framing: if you can write the score, the search is mechanical; writing the score is the science.

lenses.name: Narrative
lenses.question: What is the one sentence that makes a stranger care, and what evidence backs it?
lenses.body: Under this lens the nodes that carry the story stay lit: the surprising number, the cheap fix, the reason the actor and the beneficiary are the same person. This is the lens for winning others to the cause.

lenses.name: Operations
lenses.question: Who has to change what they do tomorrow morning, and what stops them?
lenses.body: Under this lens the question is deployment. A solved problem that nobody can act on is not solved.

lenses.name: Physics
lenses.question: What is the mechanism, what are the units, and what is conserved?
lenses.body: Under this lens a problem is restated as a question about mechanism. Nodes about matter, energy, and their transport stay in focus. Money and story blur out.

nodes.title: Rerouting inside air traffic control
nodes.statement: A flight level is not a free choice. Controllers separate traffic vertically. A contrail reroute is a request into a system built for safety, not climate.

restate.operations: What is the latency from a detected region to an approved level change, and how many such requests can a sector absorb per hour before controllers refuse them?
restate.economics: Controller workload is the scarce resource, not fuel.

nodes.source: Not in the Platt interview. Cooper's framing.
nodes.body:
## Open questions
- Is the reroute requested by the dispatcher before departure, or by the pilot in flight? [OPEN]
- How far ahead must the ice-supersaturated map be trusted for pre-departure planning to work? See [Find the ice-supersaturated regions](#node/issr). [OPEN]

## Simple baseline
Pre-departure only, using the forecast map. No in-flight changes. Simpler, and it loses the flights where the forecast was wrong.

nodes.title: Fuel cost of dropping two flight levels
nodes.statement: Flying lower burns more fuel and emits more CO2. When is the trade worth it?

restate.economics: Marginal fuel per reroute times fuel price, against the value of avoided forcing at whatever carbon price you believe. The ratio decides the program.
restate.physics: Lower altitude means denser air, more drag, and a less efficient engine operating point. The CO2 from the extra fuel is a small warming that partly offsets the avoided contrail.
restate.narrative: The cost is a rounding error on a ticket. The trick is making someone want to pay it.

nodes.body:
## What is known
Per Platt: the fuel cost is small but real. Aviation is one of the hard cases for decarbonization because batteries do not have the energy density for flight, so contrail avoidance is one of the few aviation climate levers available now.

## How you would know you made progress
A cost curve: cumulative forcing avoided versus cumulative extra fuel, ranked by [Which contrails to avoid, and the ranking metric](#node/ranking-metric). The knee of that curve is the size of the program.

nodes.title: Avoid the bad regions by dropping two flight levels
nodes.statement: The intervention is a small altitude change through a known volume of air. It costs a little fuel. Everything else is deciding which flights, and getting it done.

restate.operations: A reroute request has to fit inside existing air traffic control separation rules and pilot workload.
restate.economics: The fuel cost is small but nonzero and paid by the airline; the benefit is shared. An externality with an unusually cheap fix.
restate.narrative: Two flight levels. That is the whole intervention.

nodes.body:
## What is known
Per Platt: the regions are thin, so dropping two flight levels usually gets under them at a modest fuel cost. Because the effect is local, a country that avoids contrails over its own airspace improves its own climate, unlike CO2 where the benefit is global and diffuse.

## How you would know you made progress
Forcing avoided per kilogram of extra fuel, on real flights, using the [Forcing relative to the world without the contrail](#node/counterfactual-forcing) estimate for the flight that was not flown at the original level.

## Simple baseline
Reroute only night flights through the highest-confidence forecast regions. Measure. Expand.

nodes.title: Persistent contrails warm the planet
nodes.statement: Condensation trails behind jets sometimes persist for hours and trap outgoing infrared. The fix looks cheap. Why is it not done?

restate.physics: Under what atmospheric conditions does jet exhaust nucleate ice that persists, and what is the net radiative forcing of the resulting cirrus?
restate.ml: Given satellite imagery and weather fields, where do contrails form, and how much forcing did each one cause relative to a world where it did not?
restate.economics: Avoiding a contrail costs fuel. What is the cost per unit of avoided warming, and who has an incentive to pay it?
restate.operations: Can flights drop two flight levels through ice-supersaturated air without breaking air traffic control?
restate.narrative: A measurable slice of warming with a fix that is cheap, local, and verifiable. Why is nobody doing it?

nodes.source: John Platt, Latent Space Science interview (transcript, 2026-09-23). Paraphrased and unverified.
nodes.body:
## Why it matters
Per Platt, contrails account for roughly one percent of anthropogenic warming. Over Europe, contrail cirrus covers a few percent of the sky and adds about 1 W/m² of local forcing, against roughly 3 W/m² for all anthropogenic warming averaged over the globe.

## How you would know you made progress
Forcing avoided per kilogram of extra fuel burned, measured on real flights against a counterfactual. That needs [Forcing relative to the world without the contrail](#node/counterfactual-forcing) to work first.

## Simple baseline
Avoid every forecast ice-supersaturated region regardless of time of day. Burns fuel where it is not needed and misses the layers the weather model cannot see [Weather models miss cruise-altitude humidity](#node/humidity-forecast).

## Ways the metric gets gamed
Counting avoided contrails instead of avoided forcing rewards dodging daytime contrails that may have been cooling. See [Night contrails warm; day contrails are uncertain](#node/night-vs-day) and [Goodhart's law](#node/goodhart).

## Predict vs understand
Formation can be predicted reasonably well. Persistence cannot, because it depends on [Ice crystal shape and fall speed](#node/ice-microphysics) that nobody understands.

nodes.title: Forcing relative to the world without the contrail
nodes.statement: You can measure outgoing radiation where a contrail is. You cannot measure what it would have been without the contrail. Estimating that difference is the whole game.

restate.ml: A causal inference problem with confounders in weather, surface, and background cloud. Validate on synthetic contrails injected into real scenes, where the truth is known by construction.
restate.physics: The longwave counterfactual is tractable. The shortwave one depends on sun angle, surface albedo, and crystal habit, and stayed unsolved for two years.
restate.economics: Without this number you cannot price a contrail, so you cannot decide which ones are worth fuel to avoid.

nodes.body:
## What is known
Per Platt: the team had a working longwave counterfactual model but was stuck on the shortwave one for two years. Their internal tests injected artificial contrails into real data so the true effect was known. Their own models failed those tests. The ERA search found a simple model with a combination of confounders they had not tried, and it passed. In retrospect the model was small and sane.

## How you would know you made progress
Error on injected synthetic contrails, on scenes held out from every iteration of the search. Platt's warning applies: with a relentless search you need hidden holdouts you never look at.

## Simple baseline
Nearest clear-sky pixel at the same time, differenced. Biased by everything that made the contrail form there in the first place.

## Predict vs understand
A model that fits the observed radiances is predictive. One that gets the injected-contrail test right without having seen it is closer to descriptive, because it has to carry the mechanism [Descriptive models versus predictive models](#node/descriptive-vs-predictive).

nodes.title: Descriptive models versus predictive models
nodes.statement: A predictive model fits inputs to outputs. A descriptive model carries the mechanism, so it can extrapolate to the neighboring problem. Newton's law was about gravity, not apples.

restate.physics: Consistency with conservation laws and known facts is the prior that turns a fit into a description.
restate.ml: In data-rich, closed problems like weather or protein folding, a statistical model is enough. In low-data, non-stationary problems like climate it is not, and you cannot wait thirty years to find out you overfit.

nodes.body:
## Per Platt
A 17th-century machine learning model would predict falling apples and say nothing about planets. Weather is data-rich and its attractor is fixed, so statistical models work. Climate is the attractor itself moving, with maybe fifty data points per location, so whatever you build must be constrained by what is known. His open hope is a tool that reads all the papers and fits the data at once, constrained by both.

## In this neighborhood
[Ice crystal shape and fall speed](#node/ice-microphysics) is the low-data case. [Detect contrails in satellite imagery](#node/detect-satellite) is the data-rich case.

nodes.title: Detect contrails in satellite imagery
nodes.statement: Find every contrail, every few minutes, everywhere, from satellites that were not designed for it.

restate.ml: Segmentation on geostationary infrared imagery. Labels are hand-drawn, imperfect, and half a pixel off if you are not careful.
restate.physics: Contrails are cold linear features in the thermal infrared. The signal is there; the pixels are large.
restate.operations: Continuous monitoring is what makes a reroute recommendation checkable after the fact.

nodes.body:
## What is known
Per Platt: Google built a continuous monitoring system on weather-satellite imagery with convolutional models. They ran a Kaggle competition on it, and competitors beat the internal model partly by discovering a half-pixel offset in the labels, an artifact of whether pixel (0,0) means the corner or the center, and exploiting it.

## How you would know you made progress
Detection recall on held-out days nobody has looked at, scored against labels made after the model was frozen.

## Ways the metric gets gamed
The half-pixel story is the canonical example. Any leaderboard becomes a target and stops being a measure. Keep a truly hidden holdout [Goodhart's law](#node/goodhart).

## Simple baseline
Threshold the brightness-temperature difference between two infrared bands, then run a line detector.

nodes.title: Goodhart's law
nodes.statement: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

restate.ml: Every leaderboard, holdout, and scoring function is eventually optimized against. The defense is rigor: hidden holdouts you never look at, and re-checking the score itself.
restate.economics: Any price list gets gamed by the people it prices.

nodes.body:
## In this neighborhood
- The Kaggle half-pixel exploit [Detect contrails in satellite imagery](#node/detect-satellite).
- ERA's search finding holes in a scoring function, forcing the humans to fix the score [Map the problem to a scorable task](#node/scorable-task).
- Avoided-contrail counts versus avoided forcing [Which contrails to avoid, and the ranking metric](#node/ranking-metric).

## Per Platt
The relentless search makes this worse, not better. You now have to be more careful, not less.

nodes.title: Weather models miss cruise-altitude humidity
nodes.statement: Global weather models are excellent at the trajectory of the atmosphere for two weeks, and poor at the thin humidity layers that matter here.

restate.ml: ML weather models were trained on reanalysis data that itself has poor cruise-altitude humidity. Better skill on this target needs a new label source, not a bigger model.
restate.physics: The layers are thinner than the model's vertical grid. Sub-grid humidity structure has to be inferred, not simulated.

nodes.body:
## What is known
Per Platt: weather is chaotic past roughly two weeks, and ML weather models built from the 2018-era toolkit plus a lot of data have been a step change for trajectory prediction, including tropical cyclone tracks. That skill does not transfer to ice supersaturation because the layers are not resolved and the training data does not contain them.

## Simple baseline
Use the model humidity anyway and calibrate a bias correction against satellite detections.

nodes.title: Ice crystal shape and fall speed
nodes.statement: How long a contrail lasts depends on how fast its ice crystals grow, what shape they take, and how fast they fall. None of that is known well.

restate.physics: In an ice-supersaturated layer a few hundred meters thick, what sets the crystal habit, the growth rate, the terminal velocity, and the mixing of moist air out of the plume?
restate.ml: There is little direct data. Process models fit cubics to sparse measurements. This is the low-data regime where a statistical model cannot be trusted to extrapolate.

nodes.body:
## Why it matters beyond contrails
Per Platt: the same ice microphysics sits inside every climate model. Uncertainty here propagates into what the models say about clouds generally. Solving it for contrails pays off elsewhere.

## What is known
Per Platt: contrails dissipate as crystals grow large and fall out. Fall speed depends on crystal shape, which is not known. The mixing rate from the moist core outward is approximated, not measured.

## How you would know you made progress
A measured distribution of crystal habit and fall speed inside real contrails at several ages, that a process model reproduces without being tuned to that same data.

## Simple baseline
Spherical crystals, Stokes settling, fixed mixing rate. Wrong, but it is the linear regression of this problem.

nodes.title: Who pays, who benefits
nodes.statement: The airline pays fuel. The benefit lands mostly on the region under the flight path. Nobody in that chain currently has a reason to act.

restate.economics: An externality with a local benefit is easier to internalize than a global one. A national regulator can capture most of the benefit for its own citizens.
restate.narrative: This is the rare climate fix where the country that acts is the country that gains.
restate.operations: Someone has to be allowed to ask airlines to change altitude for a reason other than safety or weather.

nodes.source: Platt interview for the locality point, paraphrased.
nodes.body:
## What is known
Per Platt: contrail effects are local, unlike CO2, so a country fixing contrails over itself improves its own climate. That asymmetry is the political lever. The reverse asymmetry is weak: there are almost no places where contrails are confidently cooling, so nobody has a reason to want more of them.

## Open questions
- Who is the natural first buyer: a regulator, an airline that wants the story, or a carbon-credit market? [OPEN]
- Can avoided forcing be verified well enough to sell as a credit? Depends on [Forcing relative to the world without the contrail](#node/counterfactual-forcing). [OPEN]

nodes.title: Find the ice-supersaturated regions
nodes.statement: Contrails persist only inside invisible pancake-shaped layers of ice-supersaturated air, a few hundred meters tall, that can last for days. Where are they right now?

restate.physics: Warm moist air injected at the tropopause sits there and slowly dissipates. What controls its persistence, thickness, and horizontal extent?
restate.ml: Weather models do not resolve cruise-altitude humidity. Can satellite detections of where contrails actually formed, plus persistence, be used to map the layers?
restate.operations: A dispatcher needs a three-dimensional no-fly volume, updated hourly, that can be avoided by dropping two flight levels.
restate.narrative: Rock candy in the sky. The air holds more water than it can carry, and any plane that flies through crystallizes it out.

nodes.source: Platt interview, paraphrased. The ten-kilograms-per-gram figure is his and unverified.
nodes.body:
## What is known
Per Platt: the regions behave like a supersaturated sugar solution. For every gram of water or soot a jet emits inside one, on the order of ten kilograms of atmospheric water freezes out. They are pancake shaped, only a few hundred meters tall, and thought to be seeded by warm moist air injected at the bottom of the stratosphere, where it can persist for days.

## How you would know you made progress
Fraction of persistent contrails that formed inside a region the map had flagged in advance, versus outside. Track it daily.

## Simple baseline
Threshold the weather model's relative humidity over ice at cruise altitude. Per Platt this is not accurate enough on its own, which is why [Detect contrails in satellite imagery](#node/detect-satellite) exists.

## Open questions
- How does a layer's lifetime scale with its thickness? [OPEN]
- Can yesterday's detections predict today's layers? Platt says persistence is days-long, so probably. [OPEN]

nodes.title: Make the case, cheap, local, measurable
nodes.statement: Every technical piece could be solved and nothing would change unless someone tells the story well enough that a regulator or an airline acts.

restate.narrative: One number, one picture of the waffle of contrails over Europe, one sentence about two flight levels.
restate.economics: The pitch is a cost curve with a very cheap first segment.
restate.operations: The pitch has to name who does what tomorrow morning.

nodes.body:
## The argument, in order
1. Persistent contrails are a measurable share of warming [Net forcing, longwave trapping vs shortwave reflection](#node/radiative-balance).
2. The night ones are unambiguous [Night contrails warm; day contrails are uncertain](#node/night-vs-day).
3. The fix is a small altitude change [Avoid the bad regions by dropping two flight levels](#node/avoidance).
4. The benefit is local, so the country that acts is the country that gains [Who pays, who benefits](#node/incentives).

## What would kill it
A public fight over daytime contrails that might be cooling. Keep the claim narrow: night flights, confident regions.

nodes.title: Night contrails warm; day contrails are uncertain
nodes.statement: The warming is constant. The cooling happens only with the sun up and at a good angle. Which contrails are confidently bad?

restate.physics: Shortwave reflection depends on solar zenith angle and surface albedo; longwave trapping does not. When is the two-sigma bound on net forcing clear of zero?
restate.economics: If avoidance costs fuel, spend it only where the sign of the forcing is certain. Night flights are the cheap wins.
restate.operations: A rule that only reroutes night flights is simpler to adopt than one that needs a radiative model per flight.
restate.narrative: Nobody argues about the night flights. Start there.

nodes.body:
## What is known
Per Platt: many contrails, mostly at night, are warming with high confidence. Very few are confidently cooling, essentially only over the poles in polar summer, where there are almost no flights. A program that avoids only the confident cases still captures most of the benefit.

## Simple baseline
Avoid persistent contrails formed between local sunset and sunrise. Ignore daytime until the shortwave model is trustworthy.

## Ways the metric gets gamed
If the target is "contrails avoided," an operator hits it by dodging daytime contrails that might have been cooling. Score avoided forcing, not avoided contrails [Goodhart's law](#node/goodhart).

nodes.title: Net forcing, longwave trapping vs shortwave reflection
nodes.statement: A contrail reflects some sunlight by day but absorbs and re-emits outgoing infrared all day and all night. Which effect wins, and by how much?

restate.physics: Earth radiates as a blackbody near 300 K, peaking around 10 microns. Contrail cirrus has very low albedo there, so it absorbs outgoing infrared and re-emits it in both directions. What is the net of that against daytime reflection of sunlight?
restate.ml: Two effects, one observable. How do you separate the longwave and shortwave contributions from satellite radiances?
restate.narrative: The contrail is a blanket at night and a parasol by day. The blanket is on 24 hours; the parasol only when the sun is up.

nodes.body:
## What is known
Per Platt: contrails are thin white clouds that reflect sunlight by day, and are nearly black at the 10 micron wavelengths where Earth radiates, so they trap outgoing heat around the clock. Net effect is warming.

## How you would know you made progress
A per-contrail estimate of net forcing with error bars, validated against injected synthetic contrails where the truth is known by construction. That is the [Forcing relative to the world without the contrail](#node/counterfactual-forcing) problem.

## Simple baseline
Assume every persistent contrail is net warming, weighted by lifetime. Wrong for polar summer and for some daytime cases [Night contrails warm; day contrails are uncertain](#node/night-vs-day), but a usable first cut.

## Predict vs understand
The longwave side is well understood. The shortwave side depends on crystal habit and how the contrail spreads, which is [Ice crystal shape and fall speed](#node/ice-microphysics) and is not.

nodes.title: Which contrails to avoid, and the ranking metric
nodes.statement: There is not enough fuel budget or controller patience to avoid every contrail. Rank them. Then watch the ranking get gamed.

restate.ml: The score is expected avoided forcing per unit fuel, with uncertainty. Rank by an optimistic bound, not the point estimate, so the program keeps learning where it is unsure.
restate.economics: This is the price list. Every airline will optimize against it, so it must be robust to that.
restate.operations: A ranking is only useful if it can become a rule a dispatcher applies in thirty seconds.

nodes.source: Platt interview for the Goodhart and UCB points, paraphrased. The ranking framing is Cooper's.
nodes.body:
## Why it is hard
Per Platt: any metric that becomes a target stops being a good metric. Once avoidance is rewarded, the reported numbers drift toward whatever is rewarded. The defense is layered: a hidden validation set, periodic re-estimation of the counterfactual, and a rule that only counts confident cases.

## Simple baseline
Night flights through high-confidence regions first, ranked by predicted contrail lifetime. Everything else waits.

## Borrowed from ERA
Platt's search picks the candidate with the highest upper confidence bound, sometimes the fifth best on point estimate, because that is where progress is most likely. A reroute program can do the same: spend some fuel on uncertain cases specifically to learn.

nodes.title: Revisit, resolution, and spectral bands trade off
nodes.statement: A satellite can revisit often, see fine detail, or see many wavelengths. Not all three at once.

restate.physics: Orbit sets revisit; aperture sets spatial resolution; detector and cooling set spectral resolution and noise. Geostationary weather satellites take a frame every few minutes with large pixels.
restate.ml: Fuse the frequent coarse instrument with the rare precise one. Platt's team did this for CO2, using a narrow-swath precise instrument to supervise super-resolution of the coarse frequent one.

nodes.body:
## Why it is here
Every detection or mapping problem in this neighborhood inherits this constraint. Platt's CO2 example: a narrow accurate instrument on the space station provides strips of truth; the weather satellite gives coarse frames every five minutes; a learned model bridges them.

nodes.title: Map the problem to a scorable task
nodes.statement: A large share of science can be phrased as "I want a piece of code that maximizes this score." Writing the score is the creative act. The search is mechanical.

restate.ml: Given a textual description plus a scoring function, a tree search over candidate notebooks, expanded by an LLM and selected by upper confidence bound, finds a good program. The human writes and repairs the score.
restate.narrative: The scientist stops writing CSV importers and starts arguing about what "better" means.

nodes.body:
## Per Platt
ERA keeps hundreds of candidate notebooks in a tree, picks by an optimistic bound rather than the best score, grows about ten leaves at a time so the search can learn from its own history, and occasionally recombines two candidates. The scoring function usually needs several rounds of repair because the search finds ways to cheat it. Scientists using it end up spending their time on what the cost function means, which he calls the essence of the scientific problem.

## Why this node is in a contrails map
Because [Forcing relative to the world without the contrail](#node/counterfactual-forcing) was solved by exactly this move. And because this site is built on the bet that the same move works for problems that are not code.

essays.title: The scoring function is the problem
essays.author: Sample essay drafted from the Platt interview
essays.summary: What a relentless search changes about doing science, and what it does not.
essays.body:
John Platt's team at Google spent two years stuck on one number: how much sunlight a contrail reflected, compared with a world in which that contrail never formed. They had the longwave half. They could not get the shortwave half through their own tests. Then a search that [treats a science problem as code plus a score](#node/scorable-task) found a small, sane model with a combination of confounders nobody had tried, and [it passed](#node/counterfactual-forcing).

The interesting part is not the search. It is where the humans ended up. They stopped writing importers and started arguing about what the score should mean. That argument is the science. When the search found a way to cheat the score, they had to repair the score, which meant understanding the problem better.

This has a cost. A search that never sleeps will find every hole in your evaluation. The defense is not cleverness but rigor: a holdout you genuinely never look at. Platt's phrase is that the tool can slice your fingers off. The [contrail ranking](#node/ranking-metric) has the same shape. The moment it decides which flights move, airlines optimize against it and [the number drifts](#node/goodhart).

None of this replaces the person who decides whether the model is about apples or about gravity. A fit that matches the data is predictive. A model that survives a test it has never seen, because it carries the mechanism, is [descriptive](#node/descriptive-vs-predictive), and only the second kind gets you to the next problem over.

essays.title: Why nobody fixes contrails
essays.author: Sample essay drafted from the Platt interview
essays.summary: The rare climate fix where the country that acts is the one that gains, walked from physics to politics.
essays.body:
There is a kind of cloud you have seen a thousand times and never thought about. Behind some jets the white line fades in a minute. Behind others it spreads into a sheet that hangs for hours. Those persistent ones are the problem, and [they warm the planet](#node/contrails), by a share that is small in the global ledger and large for something nobody is trying to fix.

The mechanism is a blanket and a parasol. By day the sheet reflects a little sunlight. All day and all night it absorbs the infrared the Earth is trying to shed and sends half of it back down. The blanket is on twenty-four hours; the parasol only when the sun is up. So [the net is warming](#node/radiative-balance), and for the flights that happen after dark there is [no argument at all](#node/night-vs-day).

Where the sheets form is the interesting part. The air at cruise altitude is sometimes loaded with more water than it can hold, in thin pancakes a few hundred meters tall that can sit there for days. A jet flying through one is the grain of sugar dropped into rock candy syrup. Find [those layers](#node/issr) and you have found the problem.

The fix is almost embarrassing. [Drop two flight levels](#node/avoidance). The layers are thin; go under them. It [costs some fuel](#node/avoidance-cost), and that is where the story usually dies, because the airline pays the fuel and the world gets the benefit.

Except the benefit is not global. Unlike carbon dioxide, a contrail warms the region under it. [The country that reroutes its own flights improves its own climate.](#node/incentives) That is the lever. It is the rare climate intervention where the actor and the beneficiary are the same government, and it can be [verified from a weather satellite](#node/make-the-case). Start with the night flights. Nobody argues about those.
